items.title: A coin doesn't 'owe' you a head after 10 tails — but a casino does
items.claim: 10 tails in a row. Probability of the next flip being heads is still 1/2. The coin has no memory. Casinos exploit the gambler's fallacy — players betting against 'streaks' actually have no edge.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the law of large numbers help short-term?

options.text: The law of large numbers only applies to dice

LLN guarantees long-run frequency convergence to expected probability, but does NOT mean short-term deviations must be 'corrected' by reverse outcomes. Each flip is independent: past results carry no information
Tails must come back to balance heads

items.reveal_title: Gambler's fallacy and the law of large numbers (correctly stated)
items.reveal:
Gambler's fallacy: the false belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, recent 'streaks' make the opposite outcome more likely.

Monte Carlo Casino, 1913: black came up 26 times in a row at a roulette table. Players reportedly lost millions betting on red, believing the streak 'must' end. Each spin was independent; the probability of red on the 27th spin was the same as on the first (~18/37 for a European wheel, less than 1/2 because of the green zero).

LLN says: as n increases, the SAMPLE PROPORTION approaches the TRUE PROBABILITY. After 10 tails in a row out of 10 flips, the proportion is 100% tails. After a million more fair flips (with roughly 500,000 each side), the cumulative proportion approaches 50%. But this happens by SWAMPING the early streak, not by REVERSING it. The next flip after 10 tails is still 50/50.

Inverse mistake (hot-hand fallacy): assuming streaks WILL continue (sports). Actually mixed evidence — some sports skills appear to genuinely streak (basketball shooting under some studies), others don't. Distinguishing real streaks from spurious ones requires careful statistics.

Gambler's fallacy explains casino profits even when individual games are 'fair-ish'. House edges (~5% in roulette) compound over many bets; players betting against streaks don't gain anything.

The broader cognitive pattern: humans expect randomness to be uniform. Real randomness has clusters and streaks. Mistaking real randomness for 'patterns' is one of the most consistently studied errors in cognitive psychology.
items.why: Past results feel like they should influence future probabilities. They don't, for independent events. Misunderstanding this drives gambling losses, conspiracy theories, and bad predictions across domains.

items.title: If something grows at 3% per year, it doubles in 23 years
items.claim: Compound growth at rate r% has a fixed doubling time of about 70/r years (rule of 70) or 72/r (rule of 72). The doubling time doesn't change as the quantity grows. That's what 'exponential' means — proportional rate, not larger jumps.
items.prompt: Why is the doubling time constant?

options.text: For exponential growth dN/dt = kN, N(t) = N0 * e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k. Independent of N0 — the time to go from 1 to 2 equals the time to go from 1000 to 2000
Only applies to populations of bacteria

items.reveal:
Exponential growth: dN/dt = k * N. Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k.

Rule of 70/72: if k% per period, doubling time ≈ 70/k (or 72/k) periods. At 7%/year, doubles in ~10 years. At 1%/year, doubles in ~70 years. At 0.5%/year (current global population growth), doubles in ~140 years.

Exponential growth is unrealistic for long times — no real system maintains constant growth rate forever. The logistic model corrects: dN/dt = k * N * (1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity.

Logistic solution: N(t) = K / (1 + ((K - N_0)/N_0) * e^(-kt)). Starts exponential (when N << K), saturates at K.

Applications:
- Epidemics: early growth (susceptible >> infected) is exponential; saturates as susceptibles deplete (or interventions take effect). The famous 'flatten the curve' is intervening in this growth equation.
- Populations: many wild populations roughly logistic. Carrying capacity set by food, predation, disease.
- Innovation diffusion: technology adoption (smartphones, electric cars) often logistic.
- Tumour growth: early stages can be exponential; later stages limited by blood supply.

Misinterpretations:
- 'Exponential' is loosely used to mean 'fast growth'. Mathematically, it means proportional growth. A linear quantity can grow faster than an exponential one in the short term.
- Confusing exponential growth (rate proportional to value) with super-exponential (faster than any fixed exponential).
- Underestimating doubling times. Many people fail the 'penny doubling' problem: a penny doubled daily for 30 days becomes ~10 million dollars.
items.why: Exponential growth feels like 'fast growth'. Mathematically it's something specific: constant percentage rate, constant doubling time. Understanding doubling times is key to understanding epidemics, populations, finance, and Moore's law.

items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.
